title: The Fox Without a Tail
author: Hovhannes Tumanyan
short_summary: A fox drinks an old woman's milk, and the old woman catches her and cuts off her tail. Too ashamed to face her friends, the tailless fox begs for it back — but the old woman says: first bring back the milk. So begins a long chain. The cow wants grass, the field wants water, the spring wants a rope, the girl wants walnuts, the walnut tree wants an egg, the hen wants grain, and only the miller gives anything away for nothing.
extended_summary:
An old woman has just done her milking and set the milk aside when a fox comes and drinks it. The old woman catches the thief and cuts off her tail. The fox begins to plead: give me back my tail, I will sew it on and go to my friends, so that they will not call me the tailless one. The old woman sets a condition — bring back the milk you drank, and you shall have your tail.

The fox runs to the cow for milk. The cow says: bring me grass. The field says: bring me water. The spring says: bring me a rope. The girl says: bring me walnuts. The walnut tree says: bring me an egg. The hen says: bring me grain. And only the miller hands the fox some grain without asking for anything in return.

From that moment the chain unwinds backwards: the grain to the hen, the egg to the tree, the walnuts to the girl, the rope to the spring, the water to the field, the grass to the cow, the milk to the old woman. And the old woman gives the fox her tail back, so that she need no longer be ashamed to face her friends.

questions.prompt: How does the whole story begin — what does the fox do?

options: She drinks the old woman's milk
She steals an egg from the hen
She breaks the jug of milk
She carries off the old woman's hen

questions.explanation: The old woman has done her milking and set the milk aside, and the fox comes and drinks it. The whole long chain — from the cow all the way to the miller — grows out of that single mouthful.

questions.prompt: Why does the fox want her tail back so desperately?

options: She is ashamed to face her friends without it
She cannot run fast enough without a tail
She had food hidden away inside her tail
She gets cold at night without her tail

questions.explanation: She says so plainly: she will sew it back on and go to her friends, so that they will not call her the tailless one. All the running about in this tale comes not from pain or hunger but from embarrassment — a reason any child understands immediately.

questions.prompt: The old woman sets one condition: she will hand back the tail only if the fox brings back the ___ she drank.
questions.explanation: The condition is simple and fair — return what you took. But that simple condition is what drives the fox across the whole village and out into the fields, because milk does not come by itself.

questions.prompt: Put the fox's visits in the order she makes them.

items: To the cow, to ask for milk
To the field, to ask for grass
To the spring, to ask for water
To the girl, to ask for a rope
To the walnut tree, to ask for walnuts
To the hen, to ask for an egg

questions.explanation: Each one answers: first bring me the thing I need. Stories built this way are called chain tales — nothing can come back down the line until the fox has reached the very last link in it.

questions.prompt: Match each one to what they demand from the fox.
questions.explanation: Each one asks for exactly what it needs in order to live: grass for the cow, water for the field, grain for the hen. The tale shows a child that everything is joined to everything else — there is a whole world standing behind one mouthful of milk.

questions.prompt: Sort each moment by which half of the journey it belongs to.

content.groupA: The fox is still asking, and being refused
content.groupB: The fox is delivering, and being paid

options.label: The cow says there is no milk without grass
The spring says bring a rope first
The girl says walnuts first, then the rope
The hen gets her grain and gives an egg
The field gets its water and gives grass
The old woman gets her milk and returns the tail

questions.explanation: The tale runs in two directions, out and back. In the first half the fox is refused everywhere; in the second every door opens, because she now has in her hands the thing that is wanted. What changes is not the fox but what she is carrying.

questions.prompt: Why does the fox have to reach the very last link in the chain before she gets anything at all?

options: Each one must first be given something itself
Each one wants to punish the fox for stealing
They have all agreed in advance to refuse her
The old woman has forbidden anyone to help

questions.explanation: Nobody here is wicked and nobody is tormenting the fox on purpose: the cow simply has no milk if she has not eaten grass, and the field gives no grass if it has had no water. The chain only moves once somebody finally gives something away for free.

questions.prompt: Who is the only one in the whole chain to give the fox something without asking for anything back?

options: The miller
The girl
The old woman
The shepherd

questions.explanation: The miller simply hands over grain, and from that moment the chain starts to unwind in the other direction. Notice that the story is not solved by cleverness but by one person's generosity.

questions.prompt: The old woman cut off the fox's tail because she drank her milk. Was that a fair punishment? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both answers can earn full marks. A strong 'it was fair' answer notices that the fox was stealing and that the old woman honestly returned the tail the moment the milk came back. A strong 'too harsh' answer notices that cutting off a tail for one drink of milk is extreme, and that the fox then had to run across the whole country. Accept either, argued from the tale.

questions.prompt: In this tale everybody wants something before they will help. Invent one more link for the chain: who would you send the fox to, what would they demand, and why exactly that?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer keeps the tale's rule: the new link must ask for the thing it needs in order to live or to do its own work, and it must connect sensibly to the links on either side. A random demand with no reason behind it is a thinner answer.

questions.prompt: The hen says: bring me ___, and I will give you an egg.
questions.explanation: It is for this grain that the fox finally reaches the mill — the furthest point of the chain. The hen's demand is the smallest in the whole story, and without it nothing moves at all.

questions.prompt: What happens after the fox gets the grain from the miller?

options: The chain unwinds backwards, all the way to the tail
The fox forgets about the tail and goes home
The miller himself gives the fox her tail back
The fox feeds the grain to her own friends

questions.explanation: The grain to the hen, the egg to the tree, the walnuts to the girl, the rope to the spring, the water to the field, the grass to the cow, the milk to the old woman — and the tail to the fox. The tale walks the same road twice, and the second time every door is open.
